body:
Minerva investigates strange magic, questions people others are ready to trust and often pushes for action before her companions agree. She can sit beside a frightened child, tease Djö over a drink and threaten someone she thinks has betrayed them. A member of the Seekers, she shares work with Fenwick, Vessalia, Di’Trillio and Pell without making every personal conclusion company policy.

16 December 2025 · You Better Watch Out

Minerva and Gregory are the first to notice a shadow moving through the silent village street. During the fight she keeps track of the rooftop creature carrying a missing child while the party battles animated toys. Ruben’s final shot drops Krampus and the child is recovered. The scene establishes Minerva’s vigilance inside a successful communal rescue.

Her participation includes more than noticing the first movement. She moves between the houses in concealment, shatters a flying rocking horse with green magic and keeps track of the rooftop creature while the street fight continues. An explosion puts her on edge even as she controls her breathing. Her watchfulness is work she performs under pressure, alongside the others who finish the rescue.

29 March 2026 · warning without trust

Minerva attempts to deliver documents she believes describe a plan to corrupt living trees. Her companions restrain her after a breakdown in trust, while she accuses them of obstructing urgent evidence. Before the Guardians she names initials and reports the suspected plot. The priestess listens; Chief Guardian Horgrith refuses to rely on information from a party that cannot trust itself.

The Codex preserves three different facts: Minerva delivers a warning; her companions dispute her conduct and reliability; and the Guardians’ refusal is a security judgment rather than proof that her information is false.

The restraint itself is visible: she struggles bound and gagged, waits for help and is ungagged after Ryvyt apologizes for his own involvement. Her companions’ explanations do not make that coercion disappear. Minerva calls it assault and says she came to deliver information; Gregory says they restricted her to keep the mission from being put at risk.

Farkur’s confession about the earlier ship changes the encounter without making the group agree. Minerva delivers the initials and warns about corruption of the living roots, while he warns the Guardians against trusting her. Moliena receives the information; Horgrith makes the security decision to refuse further cooperation and send the company away.

Minerva leaves still insisting that the danger matters. Her later personal notes describe ignored warnings and an investigation obstructed by her former allies. Those notes explain her view of the episode. They do not overrule the quest, prove the identities behind the initials or establish that the Guardians’ defenses later failed.

29 May 2026 · Howl

On the winter forest expedition, Minerva recognizes lore about beasts drawn toward magic and afraid of fire. She investigates the attacked cabin, questions whether young Ingrid carries latent magic, and sits beside the child rather than interrogating from a distance. The later discovery of the real Timothy’s body reveals that the father at the cabin is a doppelganger; Minerva’s suspicion belongs beside, not instead of, her attempt to keep Ingrid calm.

She keeps watch while the others rest because the cabin still troubles her. When Jéane later tells her she should trust others more, Minerva rolls her eyes, smiles and concedes that she is right this time. Afterward she suggests a possible place for Ingrid at an orphanage whose keeper she knows. That is an offer of a contact, not proof of a completed placement.

The unresolved boundary

Minerva’s warning, the company’s mistrust and the Guardians’ security decision remain separate parts of the record. The initials do not identify their owners by themselves, and a rejected message is not proof that the suspected threat is false. Her later notes preserve how she understood the failure without resolving every disputed fact.

September 2026 · old notes guide a new expedition

Minerva briefs later explorers to move quietly, watch for aberrations and avoid entering or casting inside the haze. She explicitly cites Scribonia’s notes for the warning that it feeds on spells. She asks the group to report historically interesting finds to her. The briefing establishes inherited precautions and an ongoing research interest; it does not resolve the ruins’ origins or independently prove every hazard rule she repeats.

Scene evidence: 1.

The Before · returning with accumulated knowledge

Minerva’s relationship with The Before develops through repeated visits, comparisons and recruitment rather than one discovery. The existing expedition record places her among people inheriting earlier knowledge, including Scribonia’s field work, and attempting to turn it into precautions for the next party.

Guidance about dangerous haze, contamination, aberrations and reporting discoveries is practical knowledge in context. It does not make every experiment safe or establish that Minerva originated all the procedures she passes on.

Teaching and the cost of curiosity

The existing Djo history records his decision to handle dangerous material and the resulting contamination. Minerva’s later praise of his courage does not erase his choice or the bodily consequence. Encouragement, inquiry and protection can pull in different directions within the same expedition.

The account also connects her with Ryvyt’s experimental work. That connection does not establish the success of a particular experiment or make collaborators’ aims identical. Calling a source an ally does not independently establish that source’s reliability.

Olindian danger and the limits of inference

In the account of her dispute with Severina, Minerva argues that attacks and the Pirate King’s position warrant an urgent response. The claimed command structure remains her account; it is not, by itself, direct proof that the ruler ordered every attack.

Severina’s request for evidence does not prove the threat imaginary. Minerva’s frustration does not settle the disputed inference. Their disagreement continues the tension already visible in her Guardian warning: information can matter even when the way it is presented damages trust.

In the later quest meeting, Minerva openly wants the Pirate King dead and is willing to discuss working with people she distrusts. She tells Djö that ending the ruler’s power would protect children who suffered as she did. That is her stated purpose for an intended killing, not proof of an accomplished liberation or a guarantee about whoever might replace him.

Her offer of reassurance sits beside decisions about secrecy and dangerous allies. The disagreements with Severina and others retain their force: concern for people harmed by the pirates does not settle who ordered every attack or make every proposed method safe.

Persistence without a final verdict

Minerva’s vigilance, care for Ingrid and affection for Djö remain beside dangerous curiosity, threats and willingness to work with distrusted allies. The record does not assign a single verdict to all of them. The outcomes of her political plans, the full history of her mothers and the terms and consequences of the forest ritual remain open.

A library that does not answer everything

Minerva researches questions raised by her encounters and offers help at Mage’s Ruin. The available account records an unanswered appeal and only limited material in the collection. Her sense of being watched does not identify the observer. Plans to enter the Ruin are not a completed expedition.

Scene references: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

Choosing to stay when the bargain is unclear

Minerva questions the killing of the childlike figures around Selwyn and is then overwhelmed by them. After awakening she negotiates in Sylvan, asks for exact terms and offers herself as a sign of trust. She wants the others to stop attacking long enough to reach an agreement.

A child says the ritual may be permanent. Minerva asks whether she will be allowed to leave afterward, then asks again when the answer is vague. The condition she eventually receives is that she alone goes with them while the others receive the body. Their explicit assurance is that she keeps her free will.

She accepts and leaves a lock of hair with Pin, asking to be brought back if the agreement goes wrong. The figures conceal her view and create silence as they lead her away; the others obtain Selwyn’s body. Keeping free will is the assurance given. A guaranteed return time and complete knowledge of the ritual are not.

In a later Sending to Fenwick, she says she is all right and has found entry to Nerithra, where she expects to be assigned a role. The message establishes that she can send that report. The ritual’s result, her full condition and a witnessed return to the company remain unestablished.

An earlier meeting about aid

Before the later search for Selwyn, Minerva brings Fenwick, Di’trillio, Vessalia and Pell together at the Sisters of Sorrow. Their discussion weighs shelter, ships and possible destinations for Dasa seeking escape. Minerva suggests the old dwarven fortress as something to investigate, not a prepared refuge.

The meeting establishes concern and competing proposals. It does not supply the Dasa’s consent, a completed evacuation or permission to treat all Dasa as one uprising. The later quest encounter with Vey and Vaa gives the siblings their own account and corrects the assumption that their purpose is simply rebellion.

The childhood she describes, and the people she lets close

Minerva describes growing up on Olindias after her parents rejected her when the antler-like wreath appeared. In later conversations she identifies them as drow and says she survived on the streets through theft, violence and other work before her mothers took her in and taught her magic. These are her accounts of a childhood the selected quests do not independently reconstruct.

She connects that history to her anger at the Pirate King and to her distrust of gods who, she says, did not answer when she needed them. She can claim that she depends only on herself, then name exceptions: Djö, Pell and other people she has allowed close.

With Djö she is capable of gentleness. She tells him that she cannot replace his sister but will be there if he needs her. She listens over drinks and offers advice about trust. The care has a dangerous edge too: she jokes about maiming or killing someone who breaks his heart. The original conversation preserves affection and menace in the same voice.

profile.personality: Minerva is watchful, suspicious, and forceful enough to make cooperation difficult when she believes other people are underestimating danger. Yet her attention repeatedly turns toward concealed threats and vulnerable people: a shadow on a silent roof, a frightened child, an injured animal, or a familiar person whose behavior no longer fits the evidence.
profile.achievements: A persistent investigator who turns inherited knowledge into field practice while testing how much risk research can ask others to bear. Negotiates Selwyn’s release and chooses to stay with the figures, later reporting herself safe without supplying the unseen ritual.
profile.relationships: Gregory and Ruben share the Krampus rescue, while Thorn and Jéane Rose help turn the Howl investigation into a trackable sequence of evidence. Vessalia, Di’Trillio, Pell, and Fenwick are her fellow Seekers, but her conclusions remain her own rather than automatic company doctrine. The Guardians’ refusal to rely on a divided party becomes one of her clearest lessons about truth without trust.
